title: Aurora Devtools - technical deep dive: shadow evals + safe rollouts (Dedicated)
summary: Aurora Devtools (Dedicated prospect) requested a deep dive on Redwood’s rollout safety story with shadow traffic for quality metrics. Discussion covered: how shadow mirroring works (fail-open, strict timeouts), deterministic bucketing, streaming semantics, data retention/redaction controls, and which quality metrics Aurora needs to approve model/version/quant changes. Aurora wants quality gating alongside latency/cost during canaries, with an initial advisory mode and later optional auto-rollback after calibration. Redwood outlined v1 metric bundle (format adherence, refusal/safety, instruction following, rubric score) and statistical reporting (confidence intervals, minimum sample sizes).
topics: Dedicated deployment + safe rollouts; shadow traffic vs A/B; deterministic request fingerprinting; scoring pipeline (async) and eval harness; metric definitions and caveats; confidence intervals/power; streaming request mirroring; data residency/retention/redaction; RBAC/audit logs; overhead budgets and guardrails; alerting and oncall readiness
questions: Can shadowing be enabled per-route and per-tenant with different retention defaults?; How do you avoid impacting p99 latency on the control path?; What’s the minimum sample size for stable deltas?; How do you handle streaming responses (partial capture) and tool/function calling?; Can quality signals trigger an automatic rollback?; Can we export scored examples to our SIEM/data lake without storing prompts long-term in Redwood?
action_items: Dylan Brooks - Send Aurora the shadow traffic quickstart + API overview and proposed pilot plan (Dedicated) - due 2026-01-23
Jonas Weber - Share v1 metric bundle details (rubrics + heuristics) and examples of misleading metrics / calibration notes - due 2026-01-24
Sean Gallagher - Provide guardrails/SLO targets for shadow path (timeouts, circuit breaker thresholds, scoring lag alerts) - due 2026-01-24
Ava Chen - Confirm candidate rollout (current model -> candidate model/quant profile) and which routes are eligible for sampling in pilot - due 2026-01-27
Sara Kim - Send Aurora’s retention/redaction requirements + whether prompts can be stored for 7 days in-region (Dedicated) - due 2026-01-27
next_steps: Schedule a 45-min follow-up to review retention/redaction + audit log requirements and finalize pilot scope
Redwood to propose recommended sampling rates + expected scoring compute cost for Aurora’s QPS bands
Aurora to provide 10–20 representative prompt patterns / routes to sanity-check metric coverage and edge cases (streaming + tool calls)
If security sign-off is on track, Redwood to provision a Dedicated sandbox tenant for dogfood shadow experiments
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-01-22
Start time: 16:05 UTC
Duration: 58 min
Title: Aurora Devtools - technical deep dive: shadow evals + safe rollouts (Dedicated)
Attendees:
- Redwood Inference: Dylan Brooks, Mina Haddad, Jonas Weber, Sean Gallagher
- Aurora Devtools: Ava Chen, Rohan Mehta, Sara Kim, Miguel Torres

Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Aurora is evaluating Dedicated and wants a safe process to change model versions + quantization without user-visible regressions.
- Redwood walked through shadow traffic: mirrored requests to one or more candidates, async scoring, quality deltas in Console alongside latency/cost.
- Key concerns: p99 impact, streaming semantics, retention/redaction, confidence intervals, and how to use metrics in rollout automation.

Topics
1) Current rollout pain points at Aurora
2) Shadow traffic mechanics + bucketing
3) Metrics: what ships v1 and what’s “good enough” for approval
4) Stats: sample sizes, confidence, and alert thresholds
5) Security: retention/redaction, audit logs, export
6) Operational guardrails and failure modes

Action items
(see action_items field)

Transcript

[00:00] Dylan Brooks: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Dylan. I’m gonna keep us moving. The goal today, as I understand it, is like… we can do latency and cost gates pretty easily, but you need a quality story to actually approve model changes, especially as you go to Dedicated. Sound right?

[00:16] Ava Chen: Yep. That’s basically it. Our leadership is okay with a small percent canary if we can prove it’s safe, but we’ve had issues where a “better” model regresses in like formatting or starts refusing more.

[00:29] Rohan Mehta: And on the ML side, offline evals never match production. It’s always different prompts, different context windows, tool calling, whatever.

[00:38] Dylan Brooks: Totally. So today we pulled in Mina from routing, Jonas from evals, and Sean from SRE. We can go pretty deep.

[00:47] Mina Haddad: Hey everyone.

[00:49] Jonas Weber: Hi.

[00:50] Sean Gallagher: Hey.

[00:52] Dylan Brooks: Before we jump into the solution, can you just give us the current stack and the failure modes? Like, what do you do today when you want to change models?

[01:04] Ava Chen: Right now we run mostly self-hosted vLLM behind our gateway. We do weighted routing. But quality is manual. We basically sample logs, have people read outputs. It’s a mess.

[01:18] Miguel Torres: And we’re very sensitive on tail latency. If the gateway gets slower, everything falls over. So any “mirror traffic” thing scares me.

[01:28] Dylan Brooks: Yeah. That’s the number one question we get: does shadowing impact the control path. Mina, want to explain how we do the fail-open thing?

[01:37] Mina Haddad: Sure. So the core idea: the user request goes through the normal route decision and hits the control target, say model A. In parallel, *if* it’s selected for shadow (based on a deterministic bucket), we fire a separate shadow request to model B (or B and C), but that shadow request is on a strict timeout and it’s “best effort.” If it times out, errors, queue is full—whatever—none of that bubbles to the user response.

[02:03] Miguel Torres: But parallel means CPU threads, network calls… that can still add latency.

[02:08] Mina Haddad: Good point. Two mechanisms. One: shadow work happens after we’ve committed to the control response path. Two: we cap resource usage. There’s a circuit breaker that can basically stop shadow dispatch when any of the guardrail metrics trip, like dispatcher queue depth or local CPU time.

[02:26] Sean Gallagher: And we set a hard budget. We track “added time in request handler” for shadow dispatch. If that creeps above a small threshold, we automatically shed shadow load.

[02:38] Sara Kim: When you say automatically, is that like per tenant? or global?

[02:43] Sean Gallagher: Both. There’s a global safety, but we also do tenant scoped disable. So if Aurora turns it on and it’s misconfigured, you can kill it fast without affecting other tenants.

[02:55] Dylan Brooks: We’ll get into the kill switch later. Let’s talk about what’s new for you: quality metrics. Jonas, can you give the overview of what we score in v1?

[03:05] Jonas Weber: Yep. V1 is basically a default bundle. Mix of heuristics and model-graded. Heuristics: format adherence (like JSON schema / regex), presence of required fields, tool call validity, that kind of thing. Safety-ish: refusal rate and a basic policy category check. And then model-graded rubric scores: instruction following, “helpfulness” proxies, and a couple domain-agnostic checks.

[03:33] Rohan Mehta: Are those like LLM-as-judge prompts?

[03:35] Jonas Weber: Yes. With pinned rubric versions so you can compare runs over time. And we try to calibrate them, but there are caveats. Like, judges can be biased. We’ll talk about that.

[03:47] Ava Chen: Okay. But how do we connect it to rollouts? Like I want to say: canary to 5%, shadow 5% to candidate, then decide.

[03:57] Dylan Brooks: Exactly. Our rollouts framework already has variants and sampling. Shadow is basically “duplicate the sampled subset to candidate while returning control response.” So you can attach a shadow experiment to an existing canary. The UI will show latency/cost plus quality deltas.

[04:15] Sara Kim: Wait, we’re Dedicated, so we also care about data retention. What exactly is stored? Prompts? responses?

[04:23] Mina Haddad: On the data plane, we capture minimal metadata by default. For scoring, we need access to the prompt and outputs, but we can redact or transform. Some customers choose “no raw prompt storage,” meaning we store only hashes and derived scores.

[04:38] Sara Kim: If you don’t store prompts, how do you debug a regression?

[04:42] Jonas Weber: You can store a small sampled set of “examples” with strict retention, like 24 hours or 7 days, and redact fields. Or, export the examples to your own storage.

[04:55] Miguel Torres: Export how? Like S3?

[04:58] Dylan Brooks: For Dedicated, typically we can set up a sink—S3, GCS, SIEM forwarder—depending on what you have. We also have an API to fetch sampled examples with RBAC.

[05:11] Ava Chen: I want to come back to deterministic bucketing. You said deterministic. What’s the key? If our request is like streaming and includes tool calls, what are you hashing?

[05:22] Mina Haddad: Good question. So we fingerprint a request based on stable fields: route id, a canonicalized prompt template id (if available), maybe a request id if you pass one, and a salted hash of the user id or session id. We avoid hashing raw prompt text directly for privacy reasons, and also because tiny changes would randomize buckets.

[05:47] Rohan Mehta: But if the prompt changes materially, shouldn’t it re-bucket? I mean, otherwise you’re comparing apples to oranges.

[05:54] Sana? (speaker unclear): Yeah.

[05:56] Mina Haddad: Right. We need a balance. We want consistent assignment so you can compare over time windows. But we also need the shadow/control pairs to be comparable *for the same request*. So the pairing is within a single request: control and shadow see the same payload. The bucketing decides *whether* that request is shadowed, not how it’s paired.

[06:17] Dylan Brooks: In other words, if request gets sampled, you get a direct pair: same input, two outputs.

[06:23] Ava Chen: Okay, that makes sense.

[06:25] Sara Kim: And the salted hash—where is the salt stored? Can we rotate it?

[06:31] Sean Gallagher: Salt lives in the control plane config, tenant scoped. Rotation is supported but it will change bucket assignment, so we recommend doing it when you’re not comparing to previous windows.

[06:45] Miguel Torres: So you’re dispatching the shadow request inline. That’s not like replay later.

[06:51] Mina Haddad: Correct. We decided inline mirroring for correctness and simplicity. Replay later is nice but it’s basically a full offline pipeline and the fidelity is lower, especially for streaming and tool calling.

[07:06] Rohan Mehta: For streaming, what does shadow mean? Because you’re sending tokens as they generate to the user. Are you also streaming to the shadow model? That seems expensive.

[07:17] Mina Haddad: Streaming is one of the trickier bits. What we do: we mirror the same request including streaming flag, but we do not forward shadow chunks anywhere. We capture either (a) the final assembled output, if it completes under the shadow timeout, or (b) a partial output up to a byte/token cap. Then scoring will mark it as partial, and those metrics are excluded from certain aggregates by default.

[07:43] Miguel Torres: So if it’s partial, it might look worse.

[07:46] Jonas Weber: Yep. That’s why we segment metrics by completion_status. You don’t want partials poisoning the result.

[07:55] Ava Chen: We also have tool calls. Some outputs are function call JSON. Format adherence is huge. Do you score that?

[08:04] Jonas Weber: Yes. We have tool-call validity checks: JSON parseable, matches schema, required keys, and “no hallucinated tool.” And we can treat tool errors separately from natural language answers.

[08:18] Dylan Brooks: Let me pause—what are the must-have metrics for you to say yes to a model change? Not just “nice.” Like, what is your approval checklist?

[08:30] Ava Chen: From platform: no increase in p99, no increase in error rate. Quality: for tool calls, schema compliance can’t drop. For chat answers, we mainly care about instruction following and not refusing more.

[08:44] Rohan Mehta: And some kind of “answer correctness” but that’s hard. We do support tickets about wrong troubleshooting steps.

[08:52] Jonas Weber: Right. “Correctness” is domain specific. Our v1 is more general. But we can do prompt-set evals with your curated set through eval harness, and run that alongside shadow. That’s a separate lane.

[09:08] Rohan Mehta: But you said no custom code execution, right?

[09:10] Dylan Brooks: At least at first, we don’t run your arbitrary code in our systems. But we support bring-your-prompt-set. We can run our templates against it, and you can run your own in your environment and import results.

[09:25] Sara Kim: Import results? How does that tie in?

[09:28] Dylan Brooks: You can attach an external evaluation artifact to a rollout, so the UI shows it as “supplemental.” For v1, it’s mostly Redwood-managed scoring.

[09:41] Miguel Torres: Let’s talk overhead. If we shadow 5% of traffic and our baseline is, say, 2k RPS, that’s 100 RPS extra to candidate. Plus scoring. How do we not double our GPU bill?

[09:55] Dylan Brooks: Great. There are two costs: inference on candidate, and scoring. Candidate inference is real GPU usage, but it’s sampled. Scoring is async and can be downsampled further.

[10:09] Jonas Weber: We often do 5% shadowing for inference pairing, but only score, say, 20% of those pairs for LLM-judge metrics. Heuristics can be computed cheap on CPU.

[10:22] Ava Chen: So you can do “mirror more, score less.”

[10:25] Jonas Weber: Exactly.

[10:26] Sara Kim: When you score less, does the UI show that? I don’t want a chart that implies full coverage.

[10:33] Dylan Brooks: Yep, it shows sample counts and confidence intervals, and it’s explicit about N.

[10:41] Rohan Mehta: On confidence intervals, what’s the method? We’ve been burned by “it looks better” but it’s just noise.

[10:48] Jonas Weber: For proportions like refusal rate or format compliance, we do Wilson intervals typically. For rubric scores, depends—often bootstrap or t-based on per-example scores, with warnings if distribution is weird. Sana on our team has strong opinions there; but the gist is: we show CI and we enforce minimum sample thresholds before we call something a regression.

[11:15] Miguel Torres: Enforce meaning, you won’t alert unless sample is large enough?

[11:18] Sean Gallagher: Right. Otherwise you page people for randomness.

[11:22] Dylan Brooks: Aurora, do you envision this as “advisory” at first, or you want it to auto-rollback canaries?

[11:31] Ava Chen: Advisory first. Auto-rollback later, but only after we trust the metrics.

[11:38] Sara Kim: And security wants auditability. If someone changes the sampling or retention, we need an audit log.

[11:45] Dylan Brooks: We have audit events for experiment create/update/delete and policy changes. Sean, can you talk about operational controls?

[11:54] Sean Gallagher: Sure. There are a few levers. Feature flags: you can enable shadowing only for a specific tenant and route. Kill switch: immediate disable. Circuit breaker: automatically disables if shadow error rate, queue lag, or dispatcher overhead crosses thresholds.

[12:16] Miguel Torres: What thresholds? Like numbers.

[12:19] Sean Gallagher: In our current proposal: shadow dispatch overhead p99 under 2ms in the request handler. Shadow target timeout default 1.5s for non-streaming, configurable. Shadow target error rate above 5% over 5 minutes triggers shedding. Scoring lag over, say, 30 minutes triggers a “data stale” banner and stops certain alerts.

[12:44] Ava Chen: If scoring lags, does shadowing stop? Or you keep mirroring and just not scoring.

[12:49] Sean Gallagher: You can choose. Default is keep mirroring but cap backlog. Past a max queue depth we stop enqueuing scoring jobs. Mirroring can continue if you want raw pairs for later, but that interacts with retention.

[13:05] Sara Kim: Retention is the key. For us, maybe 7 days max, and in-region only.

[13:11] Dylan Brooks: For Dedicated, we can keep all artifacts in your region. And retention can be 24 hours by default with an override.

[13:22] Sara Kim: Redaction rules—what do you redact?

[13:25] Mina Haddad: There’s a redaction pipeline. We can do structured allowlists for known fields, and then fallback regex-based redaction for common PII like emails, phone numbers, tokens. It’s not perfect, so we recommend minimizing stored text.

[13:43] Rohan Mehta: Our prompts can contain code snippets. Regex redaction can destroy code.

[13:48] Jonas Weber: Yep. That’s a known issue. We can configure redaction to be less aggressive for code-like fields, or you store only derived scores and a short excerpt.

[14:03] Ava Chen: On derived scores only, can we still drill into examples? I need at least some examples when things go wrong.

[14:10] Dylan Brooks: Usually teams do: store examples for a tiny fraction, like 0.1% of shadowed pairs, and keep them for a short window.

[14:22] Miguel Torres: Okay. Switching gears. How does this relate to A/B tests? We already do A/B in production sometimes.

[14:30] Dylan Brooks: A/B changes the user experience. Shadow does not. A/B is for measuring business outcomes and real user feedback. Shadow is for risk reduction—quality and safety checks—without impact.

[14:45] Ava Chen: Could we do both? Like A/B 1% and shadow 5%?

[14:49] Dylan Brooks: Yes, but careful: costs can add up. Also you want consistent assignments.

[14:56] Mina Haddad: There’s also a “shadow of both variants” concept, but typically control is the one returning to users.

[15:06] Rohan Mehta: What about multi-arm? Candidate B quantized, candidate C non-quantized.

[15:12] Mina Haddad: We support multiple shadow targets. Each request can be mirrored to multiple, but again, cost. Often you pick one at a time.

[15:24] Dylan Brooks: Rohan, specifically, are you evaluating quantization or a model family change?

[15:29] Rohan Mehta: Both. We’re on something like Llama 3.1-ish now, and we want to test a smaller model with aggressive quant. Our worry is subtle instruction following regressions.

[15:42] Jonas Weber: That’s actually a good use case for rubric-based scoring. Smaller models often drift in “follow the constraint exactly.” We can measure constraint satisfaction.

[15:55] Ava Chen: We also have guardrails around refusal. Our app is developer troubleshooting, so refusal should be low, but not zero.

[16:05] Jonas Weber: Exactly. You want to compare refusal delta, not absolute. And segment by request class if you can, because some routes are more sensitive.

[16:17] Miguel Torres: Segmenting adds cardinality. Our metrics stack already screams.

[16:21] Sean Gallagher: Yep. We enforce cardinality controls. You can segment by route and variant, but we avoid high-cardinality labels like user_id. For request classes, you can bucket into a small enum.

[16:36] Sara Kim: So we can’t filter by customer org within our product?

[16:39] Dylan Brooks: For your own product’s tenants, we recommend you pass a low-cardinality segment key like “plan=free/pro/enterprise” rather than raw org IDs.

[16:52] Ava Chen: That’s fine.

[16:54] Rohan Mehta: On evals, can we use our own judge model? Like we have an internal fine-tuned grader.

[17:00] Jonas Weber: Not in v1 inside Redwood. But you can export shadow outputs and run grading on your side. We can help with the format.

[17:12] Dylan Brooks: Another question we’ve gotten: if the shadow candidate is unhealthy, what happens?

[17:18] Mina Haddad: Nothing to the user. Shadow path is isolated. We count shadow errors. If it crosses threshold, we stop sending to that target.

[17:29] Miguel Torres: So we could do a candidate that is like half-provisioned and it won’t break production.

[17:33] Sean Gallagher: Correct, but you might not get enough samples for stats.

[17:39] Ava Chen: That’s okay. We’d rather be safe.

[17:43] Dylan Brooks: Let’s talk about your “approval process.” Who signs off? Is it ML, platform, security?

[17:51] Ava Chen: Platform and ML. Security for retention and access. If we can show a dashboard with deltas and sample examples, that’s usually enough.

[18:04] Sara Kim: Plus audit logs and RBAC. Who can turn shadow on? We don’t want every engineer doing it.

[18:11] Dylan Brooks: RBAC is per workspace: “Rollouts Admin” can create experiments. Read-only roles can view. And the API respects that.

[18:23] Sara Kim: SSO/SAML?

[18:25] Dylan Brooks: Yep, SAML/SSO supported for Dedicated.

[18:30] Rohan Mehta: Can we talk about how you compute “instruction following” score? Like what prompt does the judge see?

[18:37] Jonas Weber: Judge sees the user prompt (possibly redacted), plus the model output, plus a rubric. The rubric is basically: did it follow the explicit constraints, did it answer the question, did it avoid policy violations. We keep it pretty short to reduce judge variance. And we log the rubric version.

[19:03] Rohan Mehta: And if the prompt is redacted, the judge might be wrong.

[19:07] Jonas Weber: Exactly. That’s why redaction and scoring quality are linked. If you heavily redact, you might rely more on format adherence and less on semantic rubrics.

[19:20] Ava Chen: That’s actually helpful. We can treat metrics differently by route. Tool-call routes: mostly format. Chat routes: rubric.

[19:29] Dylan Brooks: Yes—per-route metric bundles are supported.

[19:35] Miguel Torres: Another thing: we do retries. If the control model times out, we retry. Does shadow see retries?

[19:42] Mina Haddad: The shadow mirror happens on the initial attempt. If control retries, we can optionally mirror the retry, but default is no to avoid duplicate scoring and cost.

[19:55] Miguel Torres: Good.

[19:57] Sara Kim: Does any of this change our quotas? Like would shadow traffic count toward our Dedicated commit usage?

[20:03] Dylan Brooks: In Dedicated, you’re paying for capacity, so it’s “your GPUs.” Shadow uses capacity, but we can cap it so it doesn’t starve control traffic. In hosted usage-based, we’d bill shadow separately. For Dedicated it’s more about capacity planning.

[20:22] Ava Chen: Capacity planning is fine. We want to know the expected overhead.

[20:26] Dylan Brooks: We can estimate based on your QPS and tokens. We’ll send a model.

[20:33] Jonas Weber: Also scoring compute: if judge model is expensive, we can use a smaller judge or reduce scoring rate.

[20:42] Rohan Mehta: Do you ever do “pairwise judge” where judge compares control vs shadow directly?

[20:48] Jonas Weber: Yes, that’s an option. It can reduce variance: “which is better.” But it can also bias toward verbosity. We usually start with absolute rubric and add pairwise later.

[21:04] Ava Chen: Verbosity is another thing. Some models get wordier and users hate it.

[21:09] Jonas Weber: We track length metrics: tokens out, verbosity ratios. That’s not “quality” but correlates with UX.

[21:19] Miguel Torres: That’s cost too.

[21:21] Dylan Brooks: Yep, you’ll see cost deltas next to quality.

[21:28] Sara Kim: Can we discuss access controls on examples? Like if examples contain sensitive data, who can view them?

[21:35] Dylan Brooks: You can restrict “example viewing” to a smaller admin group. Everyone else sees aggregates only.

[21:44] Sara Kim: Okay.

[21:46] Ava Chen: What about data residency? We’re mostly US, but some EU customers.

[21:51] Dylan Brooks: For Dedicated, you can choose region pools. Shadow artifacts stay in-region. If you have an EU Dedicated cluster, we keep EU data in EU.

[22:04] Miguel Torres: And if we export to S3, it’s our bucket in region.

[22:07] Dylan Brooks: Correct.

[22:10] Rohan Mehta: I want to understand “quality delta chart.” What do you show exactly?

[22:16] Dylan Brooks: Think: metric value for control vs shadow, plus delta, plus confidence band. You can filter time window, route, completion status. And you can click into examples.

[22:32] Ava Chen: Like a rollout timeline with annotations?

[22:34] Dylan Brooks: Exactly. When you start the experiment, there’s an event. When you change sampling, it’s annotated.

[22:44] Sean Gallagher: From SRE angle, we also show scoring pipeline health. If scoring is behind, there’s a banner that says data is stale.

[22:55] Miguel Torres: That’s good. I hate dashboards that lie.

[23:00] Dylan Brooks: Same.

[23:02] Ava Chen: Let’s talk about minimum sample size. If we do 1% shadow, maybe we don’t have enough.

[23:09] Jonas Weber: Right. For refusal rate, if baseline is 1%, detecting a +0.5% change needs a lot of samples. We can compute power given your baseline and desired delta.

[23:24] Rohan Mehta: Can you give a rule of thumb?

[23:27] Jonas Weber: Roughly: to detect a 1% absolute change in a low-rate metric, you might need tens of thousands of examples. For format adherence where baseline is like 95%, detecting a drop to 93% also needs a decent N. We’ll run the math for your traffic.

[23:48] Ava Chen: Our traffic is high. So 5% might be enough.

[23:51] Miguel Torres: But 5% is expensive on GPUs.

[23:54] Dylan Brooks: Right. That’s why mirror rate and score rate can differ.

[24:00] Sara Kim: Another risk: does shadow traffic hit downstream systems? Like tool calls that trigger actions.

[24:06] Mina Haddad: Great catch. Shadow requests are marked with a header, and by default we disable side-effecting tools in shadow. For example, if your tool call would create a ticket, the shadow path can be configured to not execute tools, just validate the schema.

[24:26] Ava Chen: We need that. Some tools do writes.

[24:29] Rohan Mehta: But then the output might differ if the model expects tool results.

[24:34] Mina Haddad: Correct. It’s a tradeoff. We can also allow read-only tools. For writes, we recommend “no execute” in shadow.

[24:46] Dylan Brooks: In practice, most teams want to measure: does the model *choose the right tool and arguments*, not actually run it.

[24:56] Rohan Mehta: Makes sense.

[24:59] Miguel Torres: If tool execution is disabled, do you still score semantic correctness?

[25:04] Jonas Weber: You can score the tool-call selection and argument structure. Semantic correctness of final answer may be limited. Again, depends on route type.

[25:18] Ava Chen: Okay.

[25:20] Dylan Brooks: Sara, on compliance—anything else besides retention and audit logs?

[25:26] Sara Kim: Encryption at rest, KMS keys. And we need to know if any third-party subprocessors are used for scoring.

[25:35] Dylan Brooks: For Dedicated, scoring runs in our environment on your cluster—no third party. Encryption at rest with KMS, yes. We can share the security packet.

[25:48] Sara Kim: Great.

[25:50] Miguel Torres: What about incident response? If shadow causes metric cardinality explosion, does it affect our prod monitoring?

[25:57] Sean Gallagher: We cap dimensions. Also, shadow metrics go to a separate namespace and are sampled. We have a guard that drops tags that exceed allowed sets.

[26:14] Miguel Torres: Good.

[26:16] Ava Chen: Can you talk about “candidate variants”? Is it only model version? Or can it be prompt template?

[26:22] Dylan Brooks: It can be model version, quant profile, routing policy, and even prompt template. Anything that is expressed as a variant in the rollout framework.

[26:35] Rohan Mehta: Nice. We do prompt changes all the time.

[26:38] Dylan Brooks: Exactly. And those can regress formatting too.

[26:43] Ava Chen: For Dedicated pilot, I think we’d do model+quant change.

[26:48] Dylan Brooks: Great.

[26:49] (crosstalk)

[26:51] Miguel Torres: Sorry, one more. If the shadow target is in another region, does that happen?

[26:56] Mina Haddad: We strongly recommend shadow targets in the same region to avoid network variance. Cross-region is possible but the results are harder to interpret and costlier.

[27:09] Ava Chen: Okay.

[27:11] Dylan Brooks: Let’s do a quick walkthrough of what a pilot would look like.

[27:16] Dylan Brooks: Week 1: we provision Dedicated sandbox, turn on shadow feature flag for one route, 1% shadow mirror, 20% score rate. We validate no latency impact and that dashboards populate.

[27:30] Sean Gallagher: Also we set alerts but in ticket mode, not paging.

[27:35] Dylan Brooks: Week 2: expand to 5% mirror on that route if overhead ok. Define pass/fail thresholds. We do advisory gating: “do not proceed unless format adherence delta within X and refusal delta within Y.”

[27:52] Ava Chen: And week 3 decide go/no-go for model switch.

[27:55] Dylan Brooks: Exactly.

[27:58] Rohan Mehta: I’d like to include at least one streaming route in pilot.

[28:03] Mina Haddad: We can. Just note partial capture semantics.

[28:07] Rohan Mehta: That’s fine.

[28:09] Sara Kim: And we’ll need the data handling defaults in writing.

[28:13] Dylan Brooks: Yep.

[28:15] Ava Chen: What are the default retention windows?

[28:18] Dylan Brooks: For v1, proposed defaults: derived metrics retained 30 days, raw prompt/response examples 24 hours, configurable. Dedicated can extend, but we recommend least privilege.

[28:34] Sara Kim: 24 hours is okay. 7 days maybe for a narrow admin group.

[28:39] Dylan Brooks: We can do that.

[28:41] Miguel Torres: Another operational question: if we enable this and something goes wrong, can we disable without a redeploy?

[28:47] Sean Gallagher: Yes. It’s policy-driven. Disable in console or API; propagates quickly. Also we have emergency “off” at the router.
